Glue fills the microscopic mountains and valleys of a surface, grabs it (adhesion), then dries into tangled chains that hold onto each other (cohesion). Super glue skips the drying: moisture in the air triggers it.

lineas.texto: How does glue hold two things together, when it starts out as a liquid?
Zoom in on any surface, even one that feels smooth. It's full of mountains and valleys.
Liquid glue flows into every one of those tiny valleys and fills the gaps.
Up close, its molecules pull on the molecules of the surface. That grip is called adhesion.
White glue is mostly water. As the water escapes into the air and the wood, the glue dries.
What's left are long chains of plastic, tangled together like cooked spaghetti.
And that inner grip, glue holding onto itself, is called cohesion.
That's why you clamp it. The pressure pushes glue deep into every valley.
It also squeezes out the extra. A thin layer beats a thick one, because thick glue cracks in the middle.
Super glue is different. It has no water to lose.
It reacts with the moisture in the air, and on your skin. That's why fingers stick in seconds.
So every glue is two grips at once. It holds the surface, and it holds itself.
